objects.name: Harass
objects.description:
Summary:
Harass describes a participant acting on an identifiable target, where either the participant sought to alarm, distress, frighten, or constrain that target, or a reasonable person knowing what the participant knew, and taking the target's position into consideration, would have understood the conduct to do so. It is carried out online, offline, or across both. Harassment can be achieved through a wide variety of methods, and as such identifying the use of this Technique is not about focusing on a single mechanism. Instead, Harass is defined by an identifiable target of activity, and that the activity goes beyond annoyance or trivial upset for a person in that target's position.

Detail:
Harassment has two criteria; targeting, and intent to harass, or a reasonable understanding of behaviour as harassment.

Targeting: There was a specific target of harassment (a person, a group, an institution), and a participant acted on that target. Identifying the target is a precondition for applying the Technique; for harassment to occur, a target must have been harassed. A participant who publishes discriminatory content about no one in particular has not taken part in direct harassment, but rather a form of hate speech. A participant who publishes the same content about or sent to an identifiable person has.

Intent to harass, or reasonable understanding of behaviour as harassment: Either the actor sought to alarm, distress, frighten, or constrain the target, or a "reasonable person" knowing what the actor knew, and taking into consideration the position of the target, would have understood the conduct to do so.

The reason that harassment cannot be defined alone by an actor's intent to harass is because of cases where an actor believes their behaviour to be unproblematic, such as a stalker who perceives their unwanted attention as an act of devotion. Similarly, the reason we cannot dismiss intent entirely is for cases where an actor fails to make their target feel alarmed, distressed, frightened or constrained, despite their real intent to do so. [The UK's 1997 Protection from Harassment Act](https://legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/1997/40/section/1) is built the same way, prohibiting conduct the actor "knows or ought to know" amounts to harassment.

To assess harassment from the perspective of a "reasonable person", an analyst has to first settle two things.

What did the actor know? This is not about assessing the actor's intent, but whether with the information available to them "I did not realise this could be considered harassment" is a viable explanation for their behaviour.

For example, consider a stalker who knows they have sent hundreds of messages, knows the subject has blocked them repeatedly, and knows they have moved house. A reasonable person holding those facts concludes that the subject is frightened of them, but a stalker may decide that the subject is playing hard to get. They had the information but declined the reasonable inference, and this check takes lack of awareness away as a defence. It cuts the other way too; someone who mentions having seen an individual at a supermarket, with no way of knowing that that individual was in hiding at the time and could be distressed by this information. The 'actor' in this case is judged on what they knew, and being unaware the individual was in hiding, could reasonably have not intended their comment to have been upsetting.

What is the position of the target? Taking on the position of the subject of activity helps raise awareness of cultural or demographic considerations which could make behaviour which seems trivial to a "reasonable person" in one setting seem distressing to a "reasonable person" in another.

[Interviews conducted with 199 women in India, Pakistan, and Bangladesh found that what counts as abusive material there differs from the Western picture.](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3290605.3300232) Fully clothed photographs were considered to be threatening artefacts, where in the West it is commonly only explicit images that get reported. Examples of abuse included a participant whose account was altered to show her falsely engaged to a man she did not know, and impersonation used to humiliate women seen to have departed from local norms, including by wearing modern clothing. An NGO helpline worker in Pakistan stated that "a fully-clothed photo can lead to suicide here in conservative regions of Pakistan."

Taking an example of an AI-generated picture of a woman sitting with a man, or with her head uncovered. To an analyst who doesn't consider the cultural perspective of the target it may appear unremarkable, and the study referenced above records platforms reaching the same conclusion, declining to act because fully clothed photographs break no terms of service. However, to a person in the target's position it can lead to loss of employment, marriage prospects, and physical safety. In order to appreciate the potential for harm from such cases, analysts are asked to take into consideration a person in the target's position.

A target's failure to be alarmed, distressed, frightened, or constrained does not mean Harassment has not occurred. An analyst needs to consider the potential for distress as a result of activity for the average person in the target's position. A target who happened to be feeling resilient at the time of their harassment, or who had a higher threshold to begin with, has still been harassed, even if activity did not have a lasting impact on them.

Harassment can be conducted directly, such as an actor sending a threatening or abusive message, or it can be conducted indirectly, such as by delivering material about the target to an audience, as with a post that publishes the target's home address. Harassment can also be conducted via a third party, such as by submitting a false report to a platform, or making a hoax emergency call.

A wide variety of behaviour can be considered Harassment as long as it meets the criteria outlined above. This includes other Techniques in the DISARM Framework which aren't under the Harassment category. For example, Crowding Out Contributions to an Information Space can be done with the goal of distressing those running or using that space. If the tests for Harassment are met, then an analyst can consider the Technique as having been used as a method of Harassment.

Harassment as a Method of Information Suppression:
In early October 2016 the Philippine news site Rappler published a three-part series on social media propaganda in the country. Its chief executive Maria Ressa has [written that she then received an average of 90 hate messages per hour for the next month](https://time.com/5505458/facebook-maria-ressa-philippines/), with the attacks running to her appearance, her voice, and threats of rape and murder. Ressa and her colleagues named the pattern patriotic trolling, which an international research coalition defined as [state-sponsored online hate and harassment campaigns used to silence and intimidate individuals](https://www.canada.ca/en/security-intelligence-service/corporate/publications/who-said-what-the-security-challenges-of-modern-disinformation/chapter-8-from-likes-to-leaders-the-impact-of-social-networks-in-the-philippines.html).

Non-state movements run the same behaviour against the same kind of target. Meta's first Adversarial Threat Report, published on 1 December 2021, [announced the removal of a network originating in Italy and France which targeted medical professionals, journalists, and elected officials with mass harassment](https://about.fb.com/news/2021/12/metas-adversarial-threat-report/), using a combination of authentic, duplicate, and fake accounts to mass comment on posts in order to intimidate the people behind them and suppress their views. Meta linked the network to the anti-vaccination movement V_V, and its head of emerging harms investigations Mike Dvilyanski said [the campaign used Telegram to train recruits and to circulate word of who to target](https://www.france24.com/en/live-news/20211201-facebook-hits-anti-vaccine-campaign-harassing-doctors).

Interviews conducted with seventeen academics, journalists, and activists who had been harassed for their work found participants who [changed research agenda after harassment, left institutions, and would have left the academy altogether without support](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.11145). One professor reported first-rank doctoral students quitting the programme because they were not up to the battle. The study records the emotional cost alongside the professional one, with several participants crying during their interviews, three reporting that the FBI had warned them of a threat to their life, and one describing lasting rage at senior colleagues who watched the campaign and said nothing in public. It also records the harm spreading past the target, since harassment arrived in departmental administrators' inboxes, faculty ran contentious projects alone rather than expose collaborators, and institutions with no policy asked the harassed person to write one.

Potential Impacts:
Impacts are organised by affected party. An item may appear under more than one party where the justification differs.

Primary Target:
A1001.001: Target of Activity Defamed. Harassment campaigns routinely carry fabricated accusations, as the operation against Teacher Li did in circulating the claim that he had defrauded a woman.
A1005.006: Activity Exhausts Subject's Resources. Replacing devices and buying physical security cost money that would otherwise go to the target's own work.
A1012.009: Subject Forced to Relocate. Doxxing makes relocation the direct consequence of the act, since each newly exposed address has to be abandoned.
A1012.006: Subject Killed. False emergency reports have produced fatal responses, and [Thomas et al.](https://rist.tech.cornell.edu/papers/sok-abuse.pdf) record one swatting incident in 2017 which killed the person at the address.
A1008.005: Feeling of Anger Evoked in Subject. Anger is a common response where the target regards the attack as unjust.
A1008.006: Feeling of Anxiety Evoked in Subject. Uncertainty about what has been exposed and what will follow produces a sustained background state rather than a single reaction, which is why Teacher Li began moving frequently once his address circulated.
A1008.017: Feeling of Fear Evoked in Subject. Fear is the intended product of a threat, and three of the researchers interviewed had been warned by the FBI of a threat to their life.
A1008.018: Feeling of Horror Evoked in Subject. Applies where the material is sexualised or violent, as with the sexual imagery of Teacher Li's parents.
A1008.024: Feeling of Sadness Evoked in Subject. Several of the researchers interviewed wept during the interview and described being unable to avoid internalising the hatred.
A1010.001: Subject Disengages from Information Ecosystem. Targets stop posting or broadcasting until an attack ends, which removes them from the medium their work depends on.
A1010.003: Subject Disengages from Cause. Full withdrawal from a line of work follows where the harassment is tied to that work specifically.
A1010.005: Subject Ceases Sharing Information. Targets stop publishing, which is the outcome the suppression cases are built to produce.
A1010.006: Subject Self-Censors when Sharing Information. Researchers interviewed described avoiding contentious topics and waiting for tenure before undertaking work they expected to attract attacks.
A1011.002: Activity Restricts Subject's Freedom of Expression. False reports submitted to a platform can get a target's account suspended, which restricts expression without any prohibition.
A1011.004: Activity Restricts Subject's Academic Freedom. Applies where the target is a researcher and the work curtailed is research, such as abandoned projects and rejected grant applications.
A1011.005: Activity Restricts Subject's Media Freedom. Applies where the target is a journalist and the reporting is what stops.

People Connected to the Target:
A1008.014: Feeling of Empathic Pain Evoked in Subject. Targets suffer through watching harassment of people they care about, which is the effect the sexual imagery of Teacher Li's parents was calculated to produce in him.
A1008.017: Feeling of Fear Evoked in Subject. Relatives reached directly experience fear in their own right rather than by proxy, as Teacher Li's parents did under daily visits from security officials.

Employer, Host, or Platform Community:
A1005.006: Activity Exhausts Subject's Resources. Institutions carry the cost of responding.
A1001.002: Target of Activity Undermined. An institution which fails to protect a target is shown publicly to be unable to do so.

Wider Audience:
A1010.004: Subject Declines to Start Sharing Information. People who have not yet spoken decide not to begin. [Safeguard Defenders describes the climate of fear the Chinese Communist Party wishes to create in concerned communities inside and outside China](https://safeguarddefenders.com/en/blog/teacher-li-full-transnational-repression-story).
A1010.006: Subject Self-Censors when Sharing Information. Witnesses moderate their own output without ever being targeted themselves.
A1007.002: Activity Dissuades Action. Demonstrative harassment is aimed at the people watching, and the followers who unfollowed Teacher Li after being questioned by public security officers took exactly the action they were asked to take.
A1008.017: Feeling of Fear Evoked in Subject. Members of a targeted category recognise that they could be selected next, which is the mechanism by which category-level targeting reaches people who were never contacted.
A1009.001: Spread Hate. Racist, misogynist, and antisemitic material delivered into a live chat reaches everyone watching the broadcast, not only the streamer it was aimed at.
A1009.002: Degrade Quality of Information Ecosystem. The aggregate of many people individually withdrawing or self-censoring reduces what is available to everyone.
